name: Postural Restoration Institute (PRI)

image.caption: Comité Directivo Estatal del PRI Estado de México interiores

lead: Postural Restoration, developed by physical therapist Ron Hruska, uses breathing and positional exercises to correct body asymmetries. Users hope it leads to a more even, neutral and symmetrical posture.

The chain is breathing and asymmetry exercises, rebalanced alignment of the ribcage and pelvis, then a more neutral stance. Hruska founded the Postural Restoration Institute in 1999 to train health professionals. Published work is mostly case reports and physiology papers, and appearance outcomes have not been studied.

paras: PRI-trained therapists teach specific breathing patterns and positioning exercises, often with manual work, and give home routines to repeat. Programs run over multiple sessions.
No specific harms were documented in the sources reviewed. It is delivered by licensed professionals, and people with breathing or medical conditions may want to check with their clinician.

angle.text: PRI-trained therapists teach breathing and positional exercises aimed at correcting asymmetries, which users hope gives a more even, neutral posture. The path runs from breathing work to rebalanced ribcage and pelvis to better alignment. Published trials are few, and appearance outcomes have not been studied.

lead: Postural Restoration is a posture-based approach to physical medicine developed by physical therapist Ron Hruska in the early 1990s. In 1999 he founded the Postural Restoration Institute in Lincoln, Nebraska, to train health professionals [1]. It uses manual and non-manual exercises to reposition and retrain the body toward neutral alignment [1].

Advocates claim it improves alignment, breathing mechanics and asymmetrical movement patterns. Wikipedia states there is little strong evidence that any specific posture leads to better medical outcomes [1].

paras: PRI targets asymmetrical patterned positions and aims to restore neutrality. Breathing is central, and advocates cite diaphragm function and the zone of apposition, where the diaphragm meets the rib cage [1].

No studies found. Wikipedia's references for the topic are described as a case report, an ethnography of the PRI community, a survey of physiotherapists' views on posture and older physiology papers on diaphragm mechanics [1].
